scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is "AITA" (Are They In The Wrong). Let me start by understanding the situation fully. The next morning, the wife found her mother crying and her father looking upset. When she asked what was wrong, they initially refused to say but then accused the couple of intentionally excluding religious elements, claiming they felt "spiritually assaulted." They wanted to discuss this in December but now are insisting on having the ceremony blessed by their pastor in their city. The couple tried to compromise by planning to have it blessed where they live, but the parents insisted on it being done at their house. Additionally, the father sent a message saying "honor thy mother and father" on the wedding night, which upset the couple because they felt they weren't given the benefit of the doubt. The parents also made their financial gift conditional on this blessing, which the couple is now considering refusing, along with lessening contact. So, the question is: Is the couple in the wrong here? First, I need to consider the dynamics of the situation. The parents paid for the wedding, which is a significant financial commitment. In many cultures, this gives them a certain level of say in the wedding arrangements. However, the couple is non-religious, and the parents' sudden religious fervor complicates things. The couple agreed to include a prayer and blessing to appease the parents, but the officiant didn't follow through. This could be seen as a miscommunication or perhaps the officiant's personal stance. The parents then reacted negatively, feeling spiritually assaulted, which seems like an overreaction given that the couple had tried to accommodate their wishes. The parents' demand for a blessing by their pastor and making the financial gift conditional adds pressure on the couple. The couple's refusal to comply fully and their consideration of refusing the gift and reducing contact shows their frustration and desire to maintain their own beliefs and boundaries. On one hand, the parents paid for the wedding, which might give them some say, but on the other hand, the couple has the right to have a ceremony that aligns with their beliefs. The parents' reaction seems disproportionate, especially since the couple had already made concessions. The couple's decision to compromise by having the blessing where they live shows willingness to accommodate, but the parents' insistence on doing it in their city and making it a condition for their gift crosses a line. It's one thing to express disappointment or sadness, but conditioning a gift and demanding a specific religious ceremony seems manipulative and disrespectful of the couple's autonomy. Moreover, the parents' message about "honoring thy mother and father" adds emotional pressure, implying that the couple is dishonoring them by not complying. This can be seen as guilt-tripping, which is unfair. In conclusion, while the parents have a right to express their feelings and have some input due to their financial contribution, their reaction and demands seem excessive and disrespectful of the couple's beliefs and boundaries. The couple's decision to stand their ground and consider refusing the gift and reducing contact, while difficult, seems justified in protecting their integrity and relationship.
